title: County of Auvergne
capsule: The County of Auvergne was a feudal domain in the Massif Central of central France, named after the ancient Arverni Gauls, which passed through multiple comital families before being absorbed into the French royal domain. Auvergne hosted the pivotal Council of Clermont in November 1095, at which Pope Urban II preached the First Crusade before a crowd estimated at thousands, making it one of the most consequential ecclesiastical assemblies of the medieval West. The county came under the French crown when Count Alfonso of Poitiers — son of Louis VIII — died without heirs in 1271, reverting it by apanage law. The county title was later associated with the Valois branch of the French royal family and formally extinguished as an administrative unit in 1502, after which the region was integrated into the royal domain until the Revolution reorganized it into four départements in 1790.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The county's general extent in the Massif Central is well established through feudal records, but the shifting boundaries with neighboring counties of Velay, Gévaudan, and Bourbon at different periods are only approximately documented.
